An Independent Prep & Nursery School in Southgate
Vita et Pax is an independent preparatory school and nursery in the heart of Southgate, N14, educating children aged 2 to 11 for nearly ninety years. Founded in 1936, we draw families from right across North London — Palmers Green, Winchmore Hill, Cockfosters, Oakwood, Enfield and Barnet — who want a smaller, warmer school where their child is known by name.
Our classes are deliberately small, typically 15 to 20 children, so specialist teachers can give each pupil real attention, spot gaps early and keep the classroom calm and purposeful. Alongside a strong academic core, children enjoy a broad programme of languages, music, sport and the arts, structured 11+ preparation from Year 3, and wrap-around care from 7:30am to 6pm that fits family life.
From our Nursery at age 2, children follow a seamless path through Reception, Pre-Prep and Prep to Year 6 — and on to leading grammar and independent senior schools. Our name means “Life and Peace”, and it is the promise we keep: a happy, family school where every child can flourish.
Comparing your options? Read our guide to choosing a private school in North London, see current school fees, or book a visit.
Frequently Asked Questions
How do I apply for a place at Vita et Pax?
Admissions are open year-round. The first step is to book a visit or taster session through our admissions page, where you can meet staff, see the classrooms and ask questions. Our admissions team will then guide you through registration and the offer of a place.
Does Vita et Pax offer a nursery as well as a prep school?
Yes. Vita et Pax offers a private Nursery from age 2, with a continuous pathway through Reception, Pre-Prep and Prep to Year 6. Government-funded 15 and 30-hour nursery places are available for eligible families.
Can my child join in Year 3, 4 or 5, or mid-year?
Yes. Vita et Pax welcomes mid-year and mid-primary admissions where places are available. Many families move their children from state primaries in Years 3, 4 or 5 to benefit from smaller classes and structured 11+ preparation. Our admissions team will arrange a taster day and advise on how quickly children settle.
What are the school fees, and is funding available?
Current fees for Nursery through to Year 6 are published in full on our fees page. Government-funded 15 and 30-hour places are available for eligible 2, 3 and 4-year-olds in the Nursery, and wrap-around care from 7:30am to 6pm can be added to suit working families.
Where is Vita et Pax, and how do I visit?
Vita et Pax is at 6a Priory Close, Southgate, London N14 4AT — a short walk from Southgate Underground station on the Piccadilly Line, with on-site parking. We warmly welcome visits during term time; book a personal tour through our admissions page.

Private School North London — FAQ
What is the best private school in North London for ages 2–11?
Vita et Pax Preparatory School in Southgate N14 is an independent preparatory school for children aged 2–11. Founded in 1936, the school combines small class sizes, a broad specialist curriculum, and strong 11+ outcomes to selective grammar and independent secondary schools.
Which areas of North London does Vita et Pax serve?
Vita et Pax is located in Southgate N14 and draws families from across North London including Cockfosters, Oakwood, Winchmore Hill, Palmers Green, Enfield, East Barnet, Whetstone, Muswell Hill, Finchley, Arnos Grove, and Bounds Green. The school is accessible from Southgate Underground station (Piccadilly Line) and has on-site parking.
Is Vita et Pax an independent school or a state school?
Vita et Pax is an independent preparatory school — fee-paying, non-selective at entry, and not maintained by the state. It has operated independently since its founding in 1936. The school accepts government funding for eligible 2, 3, and 4-year-olds in the Nursery.
What 11+ results does Vita et Pax achieve?
Vita et Pax pupils consistently gain places at selective state grammars and leading independent secondary schools across North London and beyond, including Latymer School, Dame Alice Owen's, Queen Elizabeth's Boys, Henrietta Barnett School, St Michael's Catholic Grammar, North London Collegiate School, Highgate School, and others. Independent prep schools like Vita et Pax offer smaller class sizes (typically 15–20 pupils versus 28–32 in state primaries), specialist subject teaching from an earlier age, structured 11+ preparation, extended wrap-around care, and a broader enrichment programme including languages, music, sport, and the arts. Can my child join Vita et Pax mid-year or in Year 3, 4, or 5?
Yes. Vita et Pax welcomes mid-year and mid-primary admissions where places are available. Many families move their children from state primaries in Years 3, 4, or 5 to accelerate 11+ preparation. Our admissions team will guide you through the process, arrange a taster day, and advise on how quickly children typically settle.
Does Vita et Pax offer a nursery as well as prep school?
Yes. Vita et Pax offers a private nursery from age 2, with a continuous pathway through Reception, Pre-Prep, and Prep to Year 6. Children who join in Nursery benefit from a seamless, familiar environment all the way to 11+. Government-funded 15 and 30-hour nursery places are available for eligible families.

How to Choose a Prep School in North London
A parent's guide to the schools, the questions and the realities
Written for families weighing up independent prep schools across Enfield, Barnet, Haringey and Camden — by people who run one. Honest where most prospectuses are polished.
Why this decision is hard
It isn't really about the school
If you're reading this, you're probably weighing several prep schools, all of which look broadly similar on paper: small classes, smart uniforms, gleaming prospectuses, smiling children mid-experiment. After three or four open mornings they begin to blur. Almost everyone you talk to has an opinion, almost none of those opinions agree, and the cost of getting it wrong feels enormous.
Here is the honest truth, from someone who runs a prep school in Southgate: the choice between two reasonable prep schools is rarely catastrophic. Most children settle. Most schools, by Year 6, will have done well by your child if you're an engaged parent. The difference between a "good" North London prep and an "excellent" one — measured at the school gate eight years from now — is usually smaller than the difference between an engaged parent and a disengaged one.
That said, the choice still matters. It shapes the rhythm of family life for the next eight years. It shapes the kind of child your child becomes — not just academically, but socially, emotionally, in terms of confidence, friendships, and what they think school is for. And it shapes a real financial commitment — typically £100,000 to £180,000 in fees alone over an eight-year prep career in North London, before extras.
This guide tries to do three things. First, sketch the realistic landscape of independent prep schools across North London — Enfield, Barnet, Haringey, Camden — without ranking them, because rankings are mostly nonsense. Second, give you a working set of criteria, questions to ask, and red flags to watch for, drawn from twenty-plus years of running a prep school and watching how families make this decision. Third, be honest about how Vita et Pax fits in — what we offer, who we suit, and who we don't.
We don't think we're the right school for every child. We do think most parents will benefit from thinking about this decision more clearly, and that's what we've tried to make this guide do.
The North London prep school landscape
A quick orientation by area
North London has a denser concentration of independent prep schools than almost anywhere outside central London. Most fall into one of three groupings, which is a useful frame even if it oversimplifies things.
Enfield, Southgate and the Northern N postcodes
This belt — running from Cockfosters and Oakwood down through Southgate, Palmers Green and Winchmore Hill — is rich in family-scale, mid-fee independent preps. Schools here tend to be smaller (one form entry, sometimes two), with a strong sense of community and reasonable commutes for most local families. Notable schools in this corridor include Salcombe Preparatory School in Southgate, Palmers Green High School (girls'), Keble Prep in Winchmore Hill, and our own school, Vita et Pax, also in Southgate. Each has a distinct character — visit at least two to get a feel for the range.
Barnet and the High Barnet line
Heading west and north — Whetstone, Totteridge, Mill Hill, Hadley Wood — you'll find a mix of larger preps with senior schools attached and well-established standalone schools. Lyonsdown School, Lochinver House (boys', a little further north in Potters Bar), and the prep departments of Mill Hill and Belmont are all in this band. Fees tend to climb slightly as you move into the more affluent pockets of Totteridge and Hadley Wood.
Hampstead, Highgate, Camden and the inner North
Closer to central London, the prep landscape changes character. Schools like Highgate (large, prep through to senior, very academic), University College School Junior, North Bridge House, Devonshire House, The Hall, Hampstead Hill — these are bigger, often pricier, and more academically high-pressure. They tend to attract families either living in the catchment or willing to commute for the brand and the senior school link. Fees here are typically the highest in the region.
We've named these schools because parents ask, not because we're recommending or critiquing any of them. Each has families who would say it changed their child's life, and each has families who would say it didn't suit them. The job is to figure out which group you're likely to be in — and that's what the rest of this guide is about.
12 criteria that actually matter
In rough order of importance
Most prospectuses talk about facilities, trips, and uniqueness. None of those are usually the deciding factor. The criteria below are — based on what experienced parents tell us mattered, in hindsight, after eight years of prep school.
1. Class size and pupil-to-teacher ratio
The single best predictor of how well your child will be known by their teachers. Look for class sizes typically between 14 and 20 in a prep setting, with a clear ratio (often 1:8 or better in EYFS, 1:18 or better higher up the school). Ask whether the class size is the headline figure or an average — they're not the same thing.
2. 11+ destinations over the last three years
Don't just look at the school's marquee names; look at the spread. A school sending pupils to Latymer, Henrietta Barnett, Dame Alice Owen's, Queen Elizabeth's Boys, North London Collegiate and St Albans High is offering pupils a genuinely wide set of options. A school with five names that repeat year after year may be selecting heavily at entry.
3. EYFS provision (if you have a 3- or 4-year-old)
For Nursery and Reception, the Early Years Foundation Stage framework is non-negotiable. Look for a setting that takes the seven areas of learning seriously, has qualified Early Years staff, and balances structured learning with genuine play. The Reception classroom should feel calm, purposeful, and rich in language.
4. Wraparound care and the working-parent reality
Plenty of prep schools talk a good game about supporting working families and then close at 3:30pm with no after-school provision. Ask: what time do morning gates open, what time do they close, what does after-school care actually look like, what does it cost, and is there holiday club? If both parents work, this is often the deciding factor between two otherwise similar schools.
5. Pastoral care and behaviour culture
Read the behaviour policy and the anti-bullying policy. Ask what happens when a child is unkind, what happens when a child is anxious, who the form tutor is and how often parents meet them. Children spend more of their waking weekday hours at school than at home — this matters as much as anything academic.
6. School ethos and values
Most prep schools in North London were founded with a particular character — Catholic, Church of England, Jewish, secular, single-sex, co-ed. Even where the religious roots have softened, the ethos usually persists in subtle ways: assemblies, the calendar, what is celebrated and what is not. Visit and notice how the children speak to each other and to staff. That is the ethos.
7. Specialist teaching and breadth of curriculum
By Year 3 or 4, a strong prep should be offering specialist teachers for music, French, PE, art and ideally Latin or another language. This is one of the genuine differentiators from most state primaries. Ask which subjects are specialist-taught and from what year.
8. Fees, the full picture
Get a written fee schedule that includes registration or enrolment fees, termly tuition, lunches, trips, music tuition (group and individual), exam fees, wraparound care, and uniform. Ask about annual fee rises (typically 4–7% in recent years). Ask about bursaries and sibling discounts.
9. Location and commute
Map the school run honestly — peak time, real traffic. Will you walk, drive, take the bus, or share with another family? Where do other current families live? A school's catchment tells you as much about its character as its prospectus.
10. ISI inspection grade and trajectory
Read the most recent full inspection (not just the regulatory compliance visit). Look at the judgements on the quality of pupils' academic achievement and the quality of pupils' personal development. Compare to the previous report — is the school improving, plateauing or sliding?
11. What current families actually say
If you know parents at the school, ask them. If you don't, ask the school to put you in touch with a current parent in the year group you're considering. Schools that say no to that request are telling you something. Schools that say yes are usually confident in what you'll hear.
12. Onward fit, not just exam results
A school that prepares 95% of its Year 6 cohort for Latymer is brilliant — if your child is a Latymer fit. If your child is a quieter, more creative, more pastoral type, the same school may not serve them well. Ask where children who don't get into the most selective schools end up. The answer reveals what the school does for the bottom half of its cohort, which is often the more honest measure.
10 questions to ask on a school visit
Beyond "what makes you special?"
Most school tours are gentle and one-directional — Head talks, parents listen, children are paraded through nicely. That's fine, but it's also why every school sounds excellent on a Wednesday morning in October. You'll learn far more by asking the questions below, because the answers separate confident schools from defensive ones.
A confident school will answer all of these without flinching. A school that bristles, deflects, or talks around several of them is telling you something. Take notes during the visit if you can; by school four, you will not remember which Head said what.
Red flags to watch for
Trust the small details that don't add up
Comparing fees in North London
What you'll actually pay
Headline termly fees for prep schools in North London for 2026 entry typically fall into three rough bands:
Termly fees (typical range)
Annual cost (3 terms)
These are illustrative ranges, not specific school fees — schools update fees annually and you should always check the current schedule directly. Add roughly 10–20% on top of headline fees for the realistic all-in cost: registration or enrolment fees, lunches, trips, music tuition, exam fees and wraparound care. A school quoting £5,000 a term will commonly cost a family closer to £17,000–£18,000 a year once everything is added in.
Two practical points. First, ask about historical fee inflation. Independent school fees have risen between 4% and 7% a year in recent years, and that compounds. Over an eight-year prep career, fees can rise by 40% or more in real terms. Second, ask about bursaries. Most schools — including Vita et Pax — offer means-tested support to families who would otherwise struggle. Don't assume you won't qualify; many parents are surprised.
Our own current fee schedule is published on our admissions and fees page.
Application timeline
When to start, and what happens when
For Reception entry (age 4), here's the typical North London rhythm:
2 to 2½ years before entry
Start visiting open mornings. Most popular schools run them in the autumn and spring terms.
12 to 18 months before entry
Register your child at your shortlist (usually 2–4 schools). Registration fees are typically £75–£250 and non-refundable. Some schools close registration this far ahead.
9 to 12 months before entry
Taster sessions or assessment mornings. For Reception entry these are gentle play-based observations, not tests.
6 to 9 months before entry
Offer letters arrive. You'll typically have 2–4 weeks to accept, with each school setting its own acceptance or enrolment fee arrangements.
Spring/summer of entry year
Settling-in visits, uniform fittings, induction sessions. The good schools invest heavily in this phase.
For 7+ or 8+ entry into a prep, the rhythm is similar but compressed by about six months, with formal assessments (English, maths, sometimes reasoning) replacing the play-based Reception observation.
How Vita et Pax fits in
Where we sit, who we suit, who we don't
Vita et Pax is a co-educational independent prep school in Southgate, North London, founded in 1936, currently around 105 pupils from Nursery through Year 6. Most of our families live in Southgate, Palmers Green, Winchmore Hill, Cockfosters, Enfield and Barnet — typically a 5 to 20-minute commute. We sit firmly in the mid-fee band described above.
We think we're a particularly good fit for families who want:
We're probably not the right school for families looking for a very large prep with an enormous extracurricular programme, an attached senior school they want to flow into automatically, or a particular speciality (heavy sport, intensive music conservatoire-style, etc.) that bigger institutions can offer.
If any of that sounds like you, the next step is straightforward: book a visit. We'd much rather you came, looked carefully, asked us hard questions, and decided we weren't right for your child than you signed up on the basis of a brochure.
Our admissions page walks through the process in detail. The Nursery and Reception page has more on the early years. Our curriculum page explains what we actually teach. And if your child is approaching school age, our reception readiness checklist is a free interactive tool we built for parents.

The Story of Vita et Pax
Founded as part of the Vita et Pax Foundation, our school carries a remarkable heritage—one connected to Pope Saint John XXIII and the Benedictine tradition of educational excellence.
The Vita et Pax Foundation
The origins of Vita et Pax Preparatory School are intimately connected with the broader Vita et Pax Foundation, established by Dom Constantine Bosschaerts OSB (1899–1950), a Belgian Olivetan Benedictine monk. Bosschaerts was a visionary figure in the Catholic Church who maintained a close friendship and collaboration with Archbishop Angelo Roncalli—the future Pope Saint John XXIII, who would later convene the transformative Second Vatican Council.
The Vita et Pax Foundation embodied progressive ideals of Christian unity and liturgical renewal that were ahead of their time. Our school's name, derived from Latin meaning 'Life and Peace', reflects its founding ethos of Christian unity and spiritual development.
Bosschaerts came to England in 1922 to establish a branch of Vita et Pax in Eccleshall, Staffordshire. In 1936, he founded additional branches at Rochester and Cockfosters in North London, where the Church of Christ the King (Vita et Pax) still bears the foundation's name inscribed on its modernist white brick façade.
Founding and Early Years (1936–1966)
Vita et Pax Preparatory School was established in 1936 as part of the educational mission of the Vita et Pax Foundation. The school's humble beginnings saw classes conducted at two locations: Bramley Road and Heddon Court. At Bramley Road, children were taught by Miss Maura Blans, while at Heddon Court, instruction was provided by the Benedictine Nuns—establishing the school's enduring connection to the monastic tradition.
By 1938, as pupil numbers grew, the school consolidated its operations and relocated to a house on Linden Way in Southgate. However, the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 brought significant disruption. Like many London schools during the Blitz, Vita et Pax was evacuated—in this case to Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire—under the care of Sister Bede.
Following the war, Sister Bernard assumed the role of headteacher, guiding the school through the post-war recovery period and the significant social changes of the 1950s and early 1960s.
The Priory Close Era (1966–Present)
In 1966, a significant milestone was reached when the school moved to its current purpose-built premises at 6a Priory Close, off Green Road in Southgate. Sister Lucia served as headteacher during this transitional period, overseeing the establishment of the new facilities.
The school was formally incorporated as Vita Et Pax School (Cockfosters) Limited, reflecting its transition from direct monastic administration to an independent charitable structure while maintaining its foundational values and Catholic ethos.
Ten headteachers have guided our school through nearly nine decades, from Miss Maura Blans in 1936 to Mr Darren May today. The Olivetan Benedictine monks maintained a presence at Cockfosters for 77 years (1936–2013), during which time they supported the parish and school. Though the monks departed in 2013, their legacy endures in the school's values and the architectural heritage of the Christ the King church building.
Our Heritage Today
Vita et Pax maintains its Catholic identity while welcoming children from all faiths and backgrounds. The school's philosophy centres on recognising the uniqueness of each individual child, fostering their spiritual, academic, personal, and physical development within a caring community.
Our core vision remains true to the original ideals of the Vita et Pax Foundation—combining rigorous education with spiritual nurture and a commitment to peace and unity. The school maintains close links with the nearby Church of Christ the King in Cockfosters, reflecting our historical connection to the Vita et Pax Foundation.
Pope John XXIII, who collaborated with our founder Dom Bosschaerts, is remembered for convening the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965). He was canonised as a saint in 2014 and is often referred to as 'Il Papa Buono' (The Good Pope). His encyclical 'Pacem in Terris' (Peace on Earth) echoes the very values upon which our school was founded.
